events.text: The World Wide Web is released to the whole Internet from CERN
ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, is unveiled to the public
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley build the first working transistor at Bell Labs
Intel releases the 4004, the first commercially available microprocessor chip

reveal.explanation: The room-sized ENIAC was shown to the press in February 1946, and within two years the transistor that would eventually replace its valves had been demonstrated a few hundred miles away. A quarter of a century later that transistor had shrunk onto a single chip, and twenty years after that the Web arrived to connect the machines.

sources.excerpt: A press conference was held on February 1, 1946, and the completed machine was announced to the public the evening of February 14, 1946, featuring demonstrations of its capabilities.

The first working device was a point-contact transistor invented in 1947 by physicists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their achievement.
The Intel 4004, released by the Intel Corporation on November 15, 1971, was the first in a long line of Intel central processing units (CPUs).
The technology was released outside CERN to other research institutions starting in January 1991, and then to the whole Internet on 23 August 1991.
